citations.quote:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) with nonempty parameter set $\Theta$. Fix $m\ge1$ coordinate targets $\psi_i:\Theta\to\Psi_i$ and procedures $C_i:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Psi_i)$, $i\in[m]$, where $\mathcal P(\Psi_i)$ denotes the set of all subsets of $\Psi_i$. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, suppose each membership event
$$A_i(\theta):=\{x\in\mathcal X:\psi_i(\theta)\in C_i(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$ and has marginal coverage
$$P_\theta(A_i(\theta))\ge1-\alpha_i,$$
where $0\le\alpha_i\le1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\le\alpha\le1$. Then, for every $\theta\in\Theta$,
$$P_\theta\{\psi_i(\theta)\in C_i(X)\text{ for every }i\in[m]\}\ge1-\alpha.$$
Thus the family of marginal confidence sets has simultaneous coverage at least $1-\alpha$. No independence assumption is needed.

derivations.claim: For each candidate $\eta\in\mathbb R$, the membership section of either interval procedure is $\{x:\eta\in[x-9/10,x]\}=[\eta,\eta+9/10]$, a Borel set, so [F2] applies. Under $P_\theta$, the true value $\theta$ is included exactly for $k=1,\ldots,9$; hence each marginal coverage is $9/10$.

The two interval procedures are equal for every observation, so their membership events coincide and joint coverage is $9/10$. Since $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=1/5$, [F3] gives the general lower bound $1-1/5=4/5$, which this example satisfies. The equality of the two events shows that independence is not assumed.

citations.quote:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Let $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ be a fixed finite family with $m\ge1$ in a statistical experiment, and let $p_i$ be a valid p-value for $H_{0i}$ as in [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, reject $H_{0i}$ exactly when $p_i(X)\le\alpha/m$. Then, for every $\theta$ in the parameter space,
$$P_\theta\{\text{at least one true null is rejected}\}=P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)\le\alpha.$$
The bound holds for every true-null configuration, including the global null and configurations with false nulls, and for arbitrary dependence among the p-values. This is strong FWER control; it is not an FDR guarantee.

derivations.claim: Each $P_\theta$ assigns mass $1/4$ to four distinct points, so its masses sum to $1$. Under either parameter where $H_{01}$ is true, namely $\theta=0$, and under both parameters where $H_{02}$ is true, the corresponding null p-value has the law of $U$ uniform on $Q$. For every $u\in[0,1]$, $P(U\le u)=\lfloor4u\rfloor/4\le u$; hence both p-values are valid for their stated nulls by [F2].

At $\theta=0$, $I_0(0)=\{1,2\}$ and $p_1=p_2=U$. A true null is rejected exactly when $U=1/4$, which has probability $1/4$. On that event $V_0=R=2$ and $V_0/(R\vee1)=1$; otherwise both counts are zero. Thus FWER$_0=$FDR$_0=1/4$.

At $\theta=1$, $I_0(1)=\{2\}$, $p_1=1/20<1/4$ always, and $p_2=U$. A true null is rejected exactly when $U=1/4$, so FWER$_1=1/4$. On that event $(V_1,R)=(1,2)$ and otherwise $(V_1,R)=(0,1)$, giving FDR$_1=(1/4)(1/2)=1/8$. The theorem [F3] also gives the strong FWER bound $1/4\le1/2$ at both parameter values, without an independence hypothesis.
